templates.subtopic: Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S1 Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences
templates.text: Write the next two terms of the sequence [[s]], [[s + d]], [[s + 2 * d]], [[s + 3 * d]], …

templates.subtopic: Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S1 Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences
templates.text: Write the next two terms of the sequence [[s]], [[s * m]], [[s * m * m]], [[s * m * m * m]], …
templates.answer: [[s * m * m * m * m]], [[s * m * m * m * m * m]] (multiply by [[m]] each time)

templates.subtopic: Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S1 Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences
templates.text: Is the sequence [[s]], [[s + d]], [[s + 3 * d]], [[s + 6 * d]] arithmetic, geometric or neither? Explain.
templates.answer: Neither: the differences are [[d]], [[2 * d]], [[3 * d]], which are not constant, and there is no common multiplier

templates.subtopic: Describe and continue arithmetic and geometric sequences

templates.text: The $n$th term of a sequence is $[[m]]n + [[c]]$. Write down the first four terms.

templates.subtopic: Generate a sequence given an algebraic rule
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S2 Generate a sequence given an algebraic rule
templates.text: The $n$th term of a sequence is $[[m]]n - [[c]]$. Work out the 1st, 2nd and 10th terms.

templates.subtopic: Generate a sequence given an algebraic rule
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S2 Generate a sequence given an algebraic rule
templates.text: The $n$th term of a sequence is $[[m]]n + [[c]]$. Is [[t]] a term of the sequence? Show how you know.
templates.answer: [[(t - c) % m == 0|if:Yes: n is a whole number/No: n is not a whole number]]: n = ([[t]] − [[c]]) ÷ [[m]] = [[(t - c) / m|dp:2]]

templates.subtopic: Generate a sequence given an algebraic rule

templates.text: The $n$th term of a sequence is $[[m]]n + [[c]]$. (a) Work out the 50th term. (b) Which term is equal to [[m * k + c]]? (3 marks)

templates.subtopic: Explore other sequences
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S3 Explore other sequences
templates.text: Write down the first five terms of the sequence of square numbers and the next triangular number after [[t]] if the triangular numbers start 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.
templates.answer: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25; the next triangular number after [[t]] is [[t + n]]

templates.subtopic: Explore other sequences

templates.text: A sequence starts [[a]], [[b]] and each term is the sum of the previous two. Write the next three terms.

templates.subtopic: Explore other sequences
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S3 Explore other sequences
templates.text: Here are the first four terms of a sequence: [[a]], [[a + 3]], [[a + 8]], [[a + 15]]. Find the differences and describe the pattern.
templates.answer: Differences 3, 5, 7: the differences go up by 2, so it is a quadratic sequence

templates.text: A sequence has the $n$th term $[[d]]n[[c|signed]]$. Find the 20th term. Then use the $n$th term to say whether [[t]] is in the sequence.
templates.answer: 20th term: [[20 * d + c]]; [[t]] [[(t - c) % d == 0|if:is/is not]] in the sequence

templates.subtopic: Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S6 Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.text: Ali says 'the sum of two odd numbers is always odd'. Give a counterexample.

templates.subtopic: Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S6 Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.text: Mia says '[[k == 0|if:all prime numbers are odd/]][[k == 1|if:all square numbers are odd/]][[k == 2|if:all multiples of 3 are odd/]]'. Give a counterexample.
templates.answer: [[k == 0|if:2 is prime and even/]][[k == 1|if:4 is a square and even/]][[k == 2|if:6 is a multiple of 3 and even/]]

templates.subtopic: Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S6 Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.text: Ben says '$n^2 > n$ for every number $n$'. Show he is wrong by finding a counterexample.
templates.answer: When $n = 1$, $n^2 = 1$ which is not greater than $n$ (or $n = \frac{1}{[[a + 1]]}$, then $n^2 < n$)

templates.subtopic: Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.source: Y11 Foundation Autumn B4 Sequences and proof · S6 Arguments and counterexamples (E)
templates.text: Decide whether 'the product of two consecutive integers is always even' is true. Give a proof or a counterexample. Test with [[n]] × [[n + 1]]. (3 marks)
templates.answer: True: one of any two consecutive integers is even, so the product is even ([[n]] × [[n + 1]] = [[n * (n + 1)]])
